Expert Report: The Work and Torah Thought of the Gaon Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, Author of "Mishneh la-Melekh"
The present report surveys the multifaceted figure of Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, one of the great sages of Turkey in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, who combined public leadership as Chacham Bashi with extreme humility and a resolute struggle against the Sabbateans. The text focuses on his monumental work "Mishneh la-Melekh," which was edited by his student Rabbi Yaakov Culi and became a canonical commentary on Maimonides thanks to a method of analytic study that anticipated the world of modern lomdut. In addition, the article describes his contribution to the fields of thought and homiletics in his book "Parashat Derakhim," emphasizing his halakhic inclination to rule leniently by virtue of his immense erudition. Ultimately, the source seeks to illuminate the decisive influence of Rosanes as a bridge figure whose works became permanent possessions in both the Sephardic and the Ashkenazi worlds.
Expert Report: The Work and Torah Thought of the Gaon Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, Author of "Mishneh la-Melekh"
I. Introduction: The Gaon of Kushta—Historical and Biographical Background
The Gaon Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes (Rosanes, 1657–1727), known by the literary epithet "Mishneh la-Melekh" after his central work, stands as one of the most formative and influential figures among the late Sephardic sages, and in the history of halakha as a whole. His rabbinic work, which unfolded in Kushta (Constantinople) at the turn of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, profoundly influenced the method of study and halakhic decision-making for centuries to come. An analysis of his figure reveals a rare combination of extreme humility, boundless erudition, extensive communal involvement, and ideological resolve in the face of spiritual crises.
A. His Life and Environment: Kushta at the Turn of the Generations (1657–1727)
Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes was born in the Hebrew year 5417 (1657), and most of his life and activity took place in Kushta, which was at that time an important Torah and economic center in the Ottoman Empire.[1, 2] The sources note that he died on the eighth day of Passover, 22 Nisan 5487 (1727).[1] Some sources state that he was born in Izmir and died in Salonika [3], but the main shaping of his rabbinic authority was connected with Kushta. He was the son of Rabbi Shmuel Rosanes and the son-in-law of Rabbi Avraham Rozanos the Elder.[1]
Rabbi Rosanes' education was shaped in the glorious study halls of the Sephardic-Turkish world, and his rabbinic figure was built on broad foundations of classical interpretation and halakhic decision-making. He studied Torah from the great figures of his generation, among them Rabbi Shlomo Halevi the Elder and Rabbi Yosef ben Yeshayahu of Trani.[1, 3] In addition, he was a distinguished student of Rabbi Chaim Alfandari.[3] The multiplicity of these teachers, who represented different centers of gravity in the world of Sephardic halakha, provided Rabbi Rosanes with a broad and deep foundation of erudition, which enabled him to approach the complex halakhic discussions in his works with full mastery of the methods of the Rishonim and the Acharonim.
B. Public Standing and Personality (Chacham Bashi and Extreme Humility)
During his life, Rabbi Rosanes filled significant leadership roles. He served as rabbi and head of the rabbinic court in Kushta and founded a great yeshiva there.[1] He is also mentioned as the "Chacham Bashi" (Chief Rabbi) of the Ottoman Empire.[2, 4] Alongside his rabbinic roles, Rabbi Rosanes took care to support himself not from the Torah, in the tradition of the Sephardic sages. He engaged in commerce and banking, realizing a Torah ideal based on the conception of Maimonides, which extols the study of Torah combined with work.[1, 5] His economic independence enabled him to preserve intellectual freedom and halakhic authority, independent of the needs of the community or of external pressures.
One of the most prominent features of his personality was exceptional humility. Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes wrote his notes and glosses in the margins of books in fine script and without order, since he had no intention at all of publishing his writings.[3] His humility was so extreme that Rabbi Chaim ibn Attar (author of "Peri To'ar") testified that Rosanes did not want to print his works in his lifetime, "lest it be thought that his intention was to disagree and criticize."[3] Rabbi Chaim Azulai (the Chida) corroborated this, writing that he had heard from the elders of Kushta that the matter had not even entered his mind out of his great modesty.[3] The secrets of his study and his personal conduct were transmitted to the public mainly by his secretary and household member, Rabbi Yaakov Culi (author of "Me'am Lo'ez"), who noted that Rabbi Rosanes was a preacher, a supporter of the poor, a father of orphans, and a protector of all.[3]
C. The Ideological Struggle: The Front against the Sabbateans
The period in which Rabbi Rosanes was active was a stormy one in Judaism, when the Sabbatean movement, which had begun to spread a generation earlier, continued to threaten the foundations of halakha and tradition. Rabbi Rosanes stood at the forefront of the ideological struggle against this phenomenon.[4] He was a sharp opponent of Shabbetai Tzvi and the Sabbateans, and signed writs of excommunication (herem) against the movement's main disseminators, including Nathan of Gaza, Nehemiah Hayun and Chaim Malakh.[1] This resolute stand reflects his conception that depth of halakhic study and adherence to traditional methods do not contradict, but require, zealous guarding of the boundaries of Torah and halakha in the face of false and dangerous messianic moves. In this way he established himself as one who combined analytic innovation with unreserved loyalty to the tradition of halakhic decision-making.
II. His Central Work: "Mishneh la-Melekh"—Editing, Structure and the Theory of Interpretation
The book "Mishneh la-Melekh" on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah is the flagship work of Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, and he is known by its name to this day.[5, 6, 7] This book is considered one of the most classical and influential commentaries on Maimonides, and without it, it is difficult to imagine the halakhic discussion of Maimonides in the period of the Acharonim and onward.
A. The Birth of the "Unplanned Creation"
The uniqueness of the book lies in the circumstances of its writing and publication. The work was originally written as novellae on various topics [1], or, more precisely, as personal notes in the margins of books, written in fine script and without intention to publish them.[3] This approach, which stems from the author's humility [3], explains the analytic and informal character of the work: it is not a running commentary, but an in-depth discussion and investigation of the roots of halakha wherever Maimonides appears difficult or contradictory.
The foundational work was published only after the death of Rabbi Rosanes. His distinguished student, Rabbi Yaakov Culi, was the one who collected the manuscripts and his glosses, edited them and arranged them systematically as a commentary closely following the order of Maimonides.[1, 5, 7] The main source for the editing was the "books of simanim" that Rabbi Rosanes left behind, although this source was not explicitly mentioned in Rabbi Culi's introduction.[5]
Rabbi Culi is also the one who gave the book its famous name. In his introduction he explained that the word "Mishneh" refers to Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, whereas the word "Melekh" serves as an acronym for the three classical commentators on Maimonides who preceded him.[5] The transformation of a collection of private glosses into a canonical work through the student's precise editing gave Rabbi Rosanes' novellae a circulation and authority that would not have been possible had he published them himself. The author's clear and straightforward Torah thought, recorded in the "real time" of study, thus became a fundamental study tool.
B. The Methodology of the Commentary on Maimonides
The methodology of the Mishneh la-Melekh is characterized by depth, erudition and a tireless drive to clarify the reasoning of Maimonides. Rabbi Rosanes approached the discussion from an honest and objective stance, as has been said of him: "He truly and sincerely wishes to descend to its depths and to exhaust the discussion in it, asking all the necessary questions and examining the subject from all its sides."[5] This writing is not sparing with words; it encompasses all the earlier commentators on Maimonides (such as the Maggid Mishneh, Migdal Oz and Kesef Mishneh) as well as the great critical Rishonim (such as the Raavad and Nahmanides (Ramban)), and attempts to resolve apparent contradictions or to establish Maimonides' position from the Talmud and the sources of the Sages.[8]
The book Mishneh la-Melekh covers all parts of the Mishneh Torah. On Sefaria, for example, one can find his detailed discussions on the Book of Holiness (the Laws of Forbidden Relations, Forbidden Foods, and Ritual Slaughter), the Book of Separation (the Laws of Oaths, Vows, Nazirite Vows, Valuations and Devoted Property), and also the Book of Kings and Wars.[9, 10, 11, 12] In his interpretation he poses honest questions and relies on his sharpness, depth and erudition to bring him to fitting answers.[5] The manner in which the discussion is conducted and its scope are what enabled the work to attain a supreme status in later halakhic literature.
C. Summary Table: The Emergence of the "Mishneh la-Melekh"
An analysis of the process of the work's writing and editing reveals the gap between the author's original intention (not to publish) and the recognition of its importance by the next generation, which led to its becoming a foundational book.
The Process of Writing and Editing "Mishneh la-Melekh"
III. His "Torah Thought"—Between Halakhic Decision-Making and Lomdut
The Torah thought of Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes is characterized by two central axes: a halakhic inclination toward responsibility and leniency, and an analytic methodology that heralded the method of modern lomdut.
A. His Halakhic Approach: A Way of Instruction toward "Leniency"
In the description of Rabbi Rosanes' figure, it is explicitly noted that his way in instruction was "toward leniency" (to rule leniently), and this is connected to his Torah greatness: "for he was great."[3] The tendency to rule leniently in halakha is not the result of uncertainty or a desire to concede, but a reflection of a deep halakhic stance. His depth of erudition in halakha and its sources, together with his ability to analyze the roots of reasoning (as expressed in the Mishneh la-Melekh), enabled him to find grounds for leniency without harming the foundation of halakha. This approach attests to a halakhic authority of high self-confidence, capable of navigating among the opinions of the Rishonim and choosing the position that is more convenient in practical terms, when the halakhic foundations allow it. This position fits the Sephardic tradition, which in many cases prefers the responsibility of the halakhic authority over excessive stringency.
B. The Mishneh la-Melekh as a Harbinger of Modern Lomdut (Precursor to Lomdut)
Current scholarly assessment places Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes as a key figure who preceded the central figures of the period of lomdut.[5] The work "Mishneh la-Melekh" became a famous and influential book immediately upon its publication, and it is considered one of the most cited and influential books in the period of the Acharonim.[5]
The innovative and analytic features that make the Mishneh la-Melekh a harbinger of lomdut are:
Fundamental inquiry into reasoning: Rabbi Rosanes does not content himself with citing sources or with a halakhic ruling. Instead, he engages in a profound investigation of the foundations of Maimonides and his reasoning. His aim is a root clarification in which he asks essential questions about the internal logic of halakha. This manner of analysis, focused on fundamental analytic questions and on the "investigation" (cheker) of abstract halakhic concepts, preceded and influenced the methodology adopted by later masters of lomdut, such as Rabbi Aryeh Heller (author of Ketzot HaChoshen) and Rabbi Yaakov Lorberbaum (author of Netivot HaMishpat).[5]
Engagement with the rules of study: His Torah thought also dealt with methodological rules, such as the hermeneutic rules by which the Torah is expounded. For example, the Mishneh la-Melekh discusses the question of whether one may be punished for what is learned from the interpretive principle "mah matzinu" ("as we find").[5] This engagement with abstract rules of decision, not necessarily connected to an immediate ruling, is a prominent characteristic of lomdut. Sages who lived generations after him, such as Rabbi Yosef Teomim (author of Pri Megadim), continued to discuss these questions, which indicates that Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes was a pioneer in placing them on the table of halakhic discussion.[5]
The influence of Rabbi Rosanes extended beyond the boundaries of the Sephardic study hall in Kushta. Although his work was published in the Sephardic-Ottoman world, it became one of the most frequently cited latter-day works in the writings of the founders of the period of Ashkenazi lomdut in Eastern Europe.[5] Rabbi Yaakov Yehoshua Falk, author of the Penei Yehoshua, who lived far from him, already in the following generation called him "one of the great Acharonim."[5] In so doing, Rabbi Rosanes created a methodological bridge between different study halls, and proved that the deep analytic trend in the study of halakha was a pan-Jewish intellectual phenomenon of which he was among the first.
C. Analytic Table: The Mishneh la-Melekh as a Harbinger of Lomdut
The characteristics shared by the Mishneh la-Melekh and the method of study developed by the great masters of lomdut in the centuries that followed justify his standing as a "harbinger of modern lomdut."
Central Lomdic Characteristics in the Method of "Mishneh la-Melekh"
IV. His Other Works—The Intellectual and Halakhic Aspect
Rabbi Rosanes, as a multifaceted figure, did not focus only on analytic commentary on Maimonides. Two of his other works complete the picture of his thought, emphasizing the ethical-intellectual aspect and the comparative-halakhic aspect.
A. "Parashat Derakhim"—A Book of Halakhic and Aggadic Sermons
"Parashat Derakhim" is a book of sermons from the eighteenth century, written by Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, and it is one of the classical books of thought and homiletics.[7] The book contains twenty-six sermons dealing with various matters, harmoniously combining matters of halakha with matters of aggadah.[1, 4, 7] Like the "Mishneh la-Melekh," this book too was edited and printed by his student Rabbi Yaakov Culi.[7, 13]
The book reveals Rabbi Rosanes' ethical and communal thought. It deals extensively with the subjects of love of Israel, charity and kindness, the customs of Israel, the heritage of the patriarchs and matriarchs, and proper relations with other peoples.[14] These sermons, which combine the depth of halakha with words of ethics and encouragement, served as a tool of spiritual and moral support for his community in Kushta, which experienced the repercussions of the Sabbatean movements and the economic crises. His preacherly character, which was also mentioned in connection with his activity on behalf of the poor and orphans [3], found its literary expression in this work.
B. "Derekh Mitzvotekha"—The Critical Comparison in the Enumeration of the Commandments
Another important work that Rabbi Rosanes left behind is "Derekh Mitzvotekha." This book deals with the enumeration of the commandments, and presents a comparative and critical discussion among the enumeration methods of the great Rishonim: Maimonides, Nahmanides (Ramban) and the Semag.[1, 5] The book also includes critical glosses on Sefer HaChinukh.[1]
The detailed engagement with the question of the enumeration of the commandments reflects Rabbi Rosanes' consistent methodological line: the need to clarify the foundations of halakha by means of critical comparison among the great Rishonim. As in his method in the Mishneh la-Melekh, he investigates the principles that underlie halakhic decisions. Although this book, alongside other works, was sometimes bound together with the Mishneh la-Melekh, its essential importance lies in itself as a comprehensive work dealing with the architecture of the world of the commandments, thereby contributing to the methodological clarity of Sephardic halakhic decision-making.[5]
V. Influence and Legacy—Rabbi Rosanes' Place in Jewish History
Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes' standing as a Torah giant was based not only on his practical halakhic rulings, but mainly on his ability to innovate in the method of study and on the influence of his writings, which crossed geographic and methodological boundaries.
A. Immediate and Generational Reception (Reception History)
Rabbi Rosanes enjoyed exceptional esteem already in his lifetime, and this esteem intensified after his death with the publication of his writings.[5] The introductions written by his son Rabbi Avraham Rosanes and by Rabbi Yaakov Culi contain extravagant descriptions in his praise, exceptional even relative to the genre of rabbinic introductions.[5]
Recognition of his greatness arrived at record speed from the great figures of the following generations, in both the Sephardic and the Ashkenazi worlds:
Rabbi Chaim ben Attar (the "Or HaChaim"): Rabbi Chaim ben Attar, who was younger than Rabbi Rosanes, frequently called him "the great rabbi" and "the wondrous rabbi."[5, 13] He even called the Mishneh la-Melekh "the honored book."[5] These praises, from one of the great figures of Morocco and Jerusalem, attest that the canonical status of the Mishneh la-Melekh as a foundational commentary on Maimonides was recognized immediately upon its publication, and it did not require a period of slow adaptation.
Rabbi Yaakov Yehoshua Falk (the "Penei Yehoshua"): Rabbi Yaakov Yehoshua Falk, one of the great Ashkenazi halakhic authorities and masters of lomdut in Central Europe, called Rosanes "one of the great Acharonim."[5] This recognition from Ashkenazi circles of lomdut, which often tended to make little use of the books of the sages of the generations close to them [5], underscores the essential importance of the Mishneh la-Melekh. The fact that the book was among the Acharonim most mentioned and cited in the writings of the founders of the period of lomdut [5] attests that Rosanes' greatness was expressed in the straightforwardness and simplicity of his writing, which strove solely for the exhaustion of the analytic discussion.[5]
B. His Lasting Contribution to Halakhic and Intellectual Literature
Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes' contribution to halakhic literature is long-term and essential:
First, the Mishneh la-Melekh became a necessary cornerstone in the interpretive discourse on Maimonides' Mishneh Torah. It is printed in nearly every edition of Maimonides, and represents the peak of the analytic discussion of the Acharonim regarding Maimonides' method. Any deep halakhic discussion of Maimonidean topics can hardly avoid passing through the sharp analyses of the Mishneh la-Melekh.
Second, Rabbi Rosanes' historical position as a "bridge figure" is vital. He was not only an important Sephardic halakhic authority, but a key figure who advanced and influenced the analytic method of study that dominated the study halls in the following centuries.[5] In so doing, he shaped modern Talmudic-halakhic study, and ensured that institutionalized halakha would retain its authority in a period of spiritual crisis (such as the Sabbatean movement), by emphasizing intellectual depth and pure analytic discussion.
C. Summary: A Legacy of Humility and Depth
Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, the Mishneh la-Melekh, left behind a dual legacy: a halakhic-lomdic legacy from the Mishneh la-Melekh, and an ethical-communal legacy from Parashat Derakhim. His figure combines extreme personal humility (refusing to publish in his lifetime) with unprecedented Torah greatness (developing an analytic method that preceded its time). His lasting success stemmed from his intellectual honesty in striving for the root of the law, and from the combination of immense erudition with halakhic responsibility that was expressed in an inclination to rule "leniently" when this was possible out of depth of reasoning. In this way, he continues to serve as an example of a bridge between personal greatness and worldwide Torah influence.
